To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the vestibular nuclei of the acute HL cats exhibit a predominance of the two-dimensional neurons and a greater gain with clockwise rotations.

(1) one-dimensional and two dimensional neurons are found to encode head orientations in response to bidirectional rotation and (2) a greater proportion of two dimensional neurons are activated in response to CW rotations.

the coding of head orientation in bilateral vestibular nuclear neurons of cats after unilateral HL is characterized by: (1) a common spatial reference for the ipsilateral and the contralateral otolithic inputs and (2) a difference in spatial/dynamic responses between the ipsilateral and contra-lateral vestibular nuclei.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the coding of head orientations by neurons of bilateral vestibulo-cerebellar pathways.
the coding of head orientations by the bilateral vestibular nuclear neurons of the cat during OVAR.
the vestibular system and how it works.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present study has provided evidence to support the notion that the vestibular nuclear neurons are able to encode head orientations in a three-dimensional space.
, in addition to the vestibular system's role in the maintenance of balance and orientation, the vestibular system also provides the essential directional coding for the head orientations.
the present findings support the hypothesis of the existence of a bilateral vestibular network that is responsible for processing otolithic signals and for producing head orientational responses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, the vestibular nuclear neurons in the bilateral nuclei are capable of responding to bidirectional OVAR, and that the neuronal responses are not simply a result of the ipsilateral or the contralateral labyrinth but are a product of the bilateral labyrinthes.

a vestibular system that is deprived of the otolith input from the labyrinth on one side is still able to generate a head orientational response, but with an imbalance in the response patterns between the two sides.

a bilateral representation of otolithic signals is required for the vestibular nuclei in encoding head orienta-tional signals and that the vestibular nuclei on each side are capable of encoding the ipsilateral and the contralateral otolithic signals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the bilateral vestibular nuclear complex contains neurons that are sensitive to head orientation in space, and that these neurons can be classified into two categories.
